paras: The lynching of Felix Wyley was the killing of a Black prisoner by a crowd at Tiptonville, Lake County, Tennessee, on a Monday night in late July 1881. Accused of raping and murdering a young white woman, Wyley was taken from the county jail after his preliminary hearing, hanged from a tree at the edge of town and shot. The wire story ran in papers across the country, and a month later Governor Hawkins offered a $5,000 reward for members of the mob.

According to the Tiptonville Star, Mollie Curtis disappeared on the evening of the 13th while walking home along the railroad to the Keystone Lumber Company's mill on Reelfoot Lake. About a week later her remains, partly eaten by hogs and dogs, were found near the road at the corner of a field, and the Star asserted that Wyley had seized and killed her there. The wire reports named her only as a young lady named "Hall", a name the Hickman Courier later corrected to "Miss Mollie Curts."

Suspicion fell on Wyley, and the Star said he was arrested on a warrant that Thursday, while a Hickman special to the Nashville American gave the arrest as Monday. Testimony reported from the hearing placed him near the spot with a heavy club and said his washerwoman had found blood on his clothes.

On Sunday night a group of men came to the jail and demanded the prisoner from Sheriff Pittman, who persuaded them to wait for a preliminary trial. They agreed, but told him they would take Wyley on Monday night "if they had to burn the jail." On Monday three magistrates heard the case before a crowded court-house and found the circumstantial evidence strong.

Between 8 and 9 o'clock that night a crowd, described locally as "about fifty men, white and black," surrounded the sheriff and the few guards who had arrived and forced him at pistol point to unlock the jail. In the dark and the crush, another prisoner, Sam Hudson, held for murder, escaped. The crowd took Wyley first to Dan Tipton's old gin shed to question him, then about two hundred yards up a cross lane to a sycamore in the middle of the road beyond Jo. Tipton's barn.

There they drew him up and let him down repeatedly; the Hickman special said he "insisted upon his innocence," while the Star said he told a different story each time. They finally hanged him, fired several shots into his body and left it hanging until morning.

The next morning Esquire Bradford and a coroner's jury held an inquest, "rendered the necessary verdict" and had Wyley buried, though wire and Hickman reports said the body was still hanging days later. The sheriff offered a reward for the escaped Hudson, and no arrest of any member of the mob appears in the coverage. On August 29 Governor Hawkins offered $5,000 for any of the persons who had "mobbed Felix Wiley, in Lake county," along with similar rewards for lynchings at Murfreesboro and in Dyer County.

The first national reports came from a Louisville Commercial special dated July 27 and a Cincinnati dispatch of July 28, both saying 150 masked men had taken Wyley ("Wylie" in the Cincinnati version) from the jail and hanged him. Briefs ran from New Haven and Washington to Omaha, Savannah and Bismarck, with the name printed as Wylie, Wydle and "Alex. Wylie." The Washington National Republican headed its copy "Served Him Right," and the Louisville special called the proof of guilt "conclusive, but he denied it."

Nearer the scene, the Hickman Courier first printed a rumor that the man had been hanged and burned and said it was "prepared to believe the rumors." The Memphis Appeal's Tiptonville correspondent called Wyley "the Black Scoundrel," repeated claims that he had killed a man and escaped from prison, and praised Sheriff Pittman's effort to protect him. The Tiptonville Star headed its account "Retribution. A Fiendish Crime Fully Avenged" and called the lynchers "visiting statesmen," yet a week later wrote that mob law's "day is passed in civilized countries."

Accounts differ on the size and look of the mob: the wires said 150 masked men, the Hickman special about 150 unmasked men, and the two Tiptonville accounts about fifty men, "white and black." The governor's proclamation dated the mobbing July 24, the day of the first demand at the jail, while local accounts place the hanging on the following Monday night.

accounts.label: Louisville and Cincinnati wires
accounts.gist: 150 masked men took Wyley from jail and hanged him to a tree for outraging and murdering a young lady named Hall; the proof was called 'conclusive' though he denied it, and the body was still hanging.

accounts.label: Hickman special to the Nashville American
accounts.gist: About 150 unmasked men overpowered the jailer and guard, took Wyley to the outskirts of town and hoisted him five or six times to force a confession, but he insisted on his innocence; he was left hanging.

accounts.label: Tiptonville correspondent and the Tiptonville Star
accounts.gist: About fifty men or 'a number of citizens, white and black' took the keys from Sheriff Pittman at pistol point after the Monday hearing, questioned Wyley at a gin shed, hanged him from a sycamore in the road and fired shots into his body; an inquest followed next morning.

accounts.label: Early Hickman rumor
accounts.gist: A hired girl's body was found in the river and a Black man was said to have been hanged and his body burned, which the Courier said was not authenticated.

framing.detail: The National Republican headed the wire 'Served Him Right' and stated as fact that he 'had outraged and murdered a young lady'.
The Memphis Appeal's local dispatch called Wyley 'the Black Scoundrel' and 'black fiend', recounted unverified claims about his past, and praised Sheriff Pittman for trying to do his duty.
The Tiptonville Star headed its account 'Retribution. A Fiendish Crime Fully Avenged' and called the mob 'visiting statesmen', but later wrote that mob law's day 'is passed in civilized countries'.
The Hickman Courier's first item said the people below the river should not show mercy to 'such fiends' and that it was 'prepared to believe the rumors'.
Northern and Western papers ran the wire as a brief under heads such as 'A Colored Murderer Lynched', 'Lynched' and 'Taken from Jail and Lynched'.
The Morristown Gazette reported the governor's reward as an effort 'to put a stop to mob law'.
